system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 1 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 18-28 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2193-11-26 18:11:00 to 2193-11-27 16:30:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis C, hepatocellular carcinoma, and type 2 diabetes, was admitted from her primary care office due to persistent hyperglycemia with blood sugars ranging from 250 to 400 despite adherence to her insulin regimen. She also reported increased lethargy and urinary frequency. Evaluation revealed patchy opacities on chest X-ray concerning for early pneumonia, and she was started on levofloxacin. Urinalysis showed bacteria, but the culture was contaminated and not actionable. Her blood glucose improved with insulin regimen adjustments managed by the diabetes team. She remained stable, with no respiratory symptoms or fever, and was discharged home on a three-day course of oral levofloxacin, continued insulin with an increased sliding scale, and discontinuation of ferrous gluconate. A visiting nurse was arranged for home support, and follow-up was scheduled with her hepatologist and primary care provider.
problems: Pneumonia, organism unspecified
Malignant neoplasm of liver, primary
Chronic hepatitis C without mention of hepatic coma
Cirrhosis of liver without mention of alcohol
Pancytopenia
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Epilepsy, unspecified, without mention of intractable epilepsy
Anemia, unspecified
Antiviral drugs causing adverse effects in therapeutic use
Esophageal reflux
Disorder of bone and cartilage, unspecified
Peptic ulcer of unspecified site, unspecified as acute or chronic, without mention of hemorrhage or perforation, without mention of obstruction
Calculus of gallbladder without mention of cholecystitis, without mention of obstruction
Other postprocedural status

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you came in this morning feeling confused and shaky?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I didn’t eat breakfast and didn’t take my insulin. Then I started sweating and feeling really weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We checked your labs and found your potassium was quite high at 6.2, and your sodium was low. We gave you something called Kayexalate in the ER to help bring the potassium down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. Is that dangerous? I’ve been eating a lot of bananas and oranges lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, those are high in potassium. With your liver condition and the spironolactone you're on, it can build up. That likely contributed to the high level. Your EKG didn’t show any dangerous changes, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I also felt confused. Was that from the potassium or my liver?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We considered several things—your liver, infection, or electrolytes. But since you hadn’t eaten or taken insulin, low blood sugar is the most likely cause. Your mental status is much better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did finish my Bactrim for the UTI yesterday. Could that have affected my potassium?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, Bactrim can raise potassium, especially with other factors. Since you’ve completed the course, we’re stopping it. That will help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my sodium? It was low too, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your sodium was 132. That’s common with cirrhosis. We’re not giving IV fluids because your body holds onto water. It’s improved to 138 now, which is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also scheduled your CyberKnife treatment for tomorrow morning at 9:30. It’s important to continue that for your liver tumor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been worried about missing it. Is it safe to go home after?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s outpatient. You’ll be monitored afterward. We’ll discharge you tomorrow once we confirm your labs are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat labs show your potassium is now 4.6 and sodium is normal. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What changes should I make to my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re reducing your spironolactone from 100 mg to 25 mg daily and adding Lasix 20 mg to help balance your fluids and protect your potassium. And stop the Bactrim—you’re done with it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any other warnings I should know about?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or go to the ER if you have fever over 101, chest pain, shortness of breath, or abdominal pain. And if your blood sugar drops below 70, eat some juice or candy right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll keep eating less banana, I promise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good start. We’ll also send a visiting nurse to check on you at home. Make sure to keep all your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re discharging you soon. Just sign the papers, and the nurse will go over your updated medication list one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will my confusion come back if I skip meals?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could. Skipping insulin or meals can drop your sugar and affect your thinking. Please eat regularly and take your insulin as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be more careful. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing great. Just keep up with your diet, meds, and appointments. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at the next visit.

summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis C, hepatocellular carcinoma, and type 2 diabetes, was admitted after presenting with confusion and shakiness. Initial labs revealed hyperkalemia (K 6.2) and hyponatremia (Na 132), likely due to dietary indiscretion, spironolactone, and insulin omission. She was treated with Kayexalate in the ED, and her potassium normalized. Her confusion resolved with improved intake and glucose control. She completed a course of Bactrim for a UTI, which was discontinued. She underwent CyberKnife therapy as part of her outpatient cancer treatment plan. She was discharged on reduced-dose spironolactone, new Lasix, and continued home medications with education on low-potassium diet and symptom monitoring. Her condition was stable at discharge.
